title: A commit (a snapshot stamped with an id and linked to its parent)
definition: A commit is a photo of your entire project at one instant. When you commit, git saves the state of all your files, stamps it with a unique id, and links it back to the commit taken just before it. So every commit knows its parent — the version right before it.

slides.narration: A commit (a snapshot stamped with an id and linked to its parent)

slides.caption: A commit photographs your whole project.
slides.narration: A commit is a photo of your entire project at one instant. Here git captures every file — app.py, index.html, style.css — exactly as they are right now.

slides.caption: It gets stamped with a unique id.
slides.narration: Git stamps that snapshot with a unique id, a1b3f7. That id is how you point back to this exact version later.

slides.caption: The commit taken just before still exists.
slides.narration: This isn't the first snapshot. The commit taken just before it, 9c2e0d, is still sitting there with its own copy of every file.

slides.caption: Each commit links back to its parent.
slides.narration: The new commit links back to that earlier one — its parent. Every commit knows the exact version that came right before it.

slides.caption: Follow the parents back for the full history.
slides.narration: And the parent has a parent, and so on. Follow the chain back and you walk through the project's entire history, one snapshot at a time.
